comp.schema.why: The instructions for every available tool go along with every step, even when the tool is never used.
comp.rebuild.why: After {ttl} without a step, Anthropic drops the cache. The next step then writes the whole history again, and writing costs several times as much as reading.
comp.break.why: The cache was lost although the last step had just happened, and the history had to be written again. Hermes causes this itself when the start of the prompt changes between two steps, not your usage. Only visible where Hermes' log has real numbers per step.
comp.think.why: Claude's reasoning before replies and tool calls. It is billed as output, the most expensive kind of token, and stays in the history afterwards.
comp.reply.why: The text Hermes writes back to you.
comp.user.why: What you write, including forwarded texts.
comp.sub.why: Helper agents Hermes starts for subtasks. Each one has its own history.
comp.other.why: Calls for which Hermes saved no messages.
comp.task:background_review.why: After replies Hermes reads the history a second time to maintain memory and skills.
comp.task:compression.why: Summarizes histories that got too long.
comp.task:approval.why: Has risky commands checked before they run.
comp.task:title: Title generation
comp.tool:skill_view.why: Content of the skills Hermes loads. It stays in the history and is read again at every later step.
label.tool.why: What {name} returns, plus the commands for it. Stays in the history and is read again at every later step.
label.skill.why: Skill content that stays in the history after loading.
label.inj.why: Attaches itself to each of your messages and stays in the history afterwards.
label.sys.why: Fixed part of the system prompt, sent with every step.
label.task.why: A task Hermes runs on its own next to the chat.

ov.eats.hint: Every step sends the complete history so far to Claude. Whatever is in it once, including every tool result, costs again at every later step. Percent and amounts are based on API prices, the same way Anthropic measures your subscription limit.
ov.logged: For {p} of the steps Hermes' log had real cache numbers per step. For the rest the cache is recalculated with the pause rule.
ov.save.hint: Calculated from your real data. Percentages refer to the selected period.

ov.guard: Budget guard: {names} paused until the week has room again.
tip.ttl1h: Keep the cache for an hour
tip.ttl1h.text: With prompt_caching: cache_ttl: 1h in config.yaml Anthropic keeps the cache for an hour instead of 5 minutes. Writing then costs 1.6 times as much, but pauses under an hour no longer trigger a rebuild. Recalculated with your real gaps between steps: about {p} less.
tip.ttl5m.text: With your gaps between steps the 5-minute setting would be about {p} cheaper than 1 hour.
tip.break.text: {p} of the cost came from the cache being lost without a pause, so the history had to be written again. This happens inside Hermes when the start of the prompt changes between two steps. Finding the cause there would be the biggest lever, and it changes nothing about how you work.
tip.unused.text: {n} tools were not used once in this period, but their descriptions still cost {p}. Most expensive: {top}. Turn them off with hermes tools.
tip.long: Start fresh when the topic changes
tip.long.text: {p} of the cost came from steps that had to read more than {n} tokens of history. Every step reads the whole history again, so a session gets more expensive over time. /new for a new topic helps the most.
tip.think.text: Claude's reasoning makes up {p}. config.yaml sets agent.reasoning_effort: {effort}{highest}. One level lower Claude thinks shorter and saves output, but may lose quality on hard tasks.
tip.review: Run the background review less often
tip.review.text: The background review cost {p}. It runs with its own prompt and writes the whole history into the cache again. A higher memory.nudge_interval and skills.creation_nudge_interval make it run less often, auxiliary.background_review.enabled: false turns it off.
tip.tool.any: Everything {name} returns is read again at every later step.
tip.tool.terminal: Long command output stays in the history and is read again at every later step. Trimming output with head, tail or grep saves the most here.
tip.tool.browser_exec: Page content and screenshots from the browser are large. Read out only the text you need.
tip.tool.session_search: Hits from old sessions bring a lot of text. Search with a smaller limit.
tip.tool.read_file: Reading whole files is expensive. Fetch only the lines you need with offset and limit.
tip.tool.vision_analyze: Images cost many tokens and stay in the history afterwards.
tip.cron.text: This cron job cost {p}. Run it less often or shorten its prompt.
tip.inj.text: What this plugin attaches to every message cost {p}.

det.breaks.hint: Each break without a pause, sorted by its likely cause. The cost is the history that had to be written again.
det.how.text: Hermes stores the real token counts from Anthropic for every session: fresh input, read from cache, written to cache, output. Together with the official price list this gives the exact API value of every session. To split it up, every session is replayed step by step: what was in the history at that moment, what was new, and whether the cache had expired after a pause of more than {ttl}. Where Hermes' agent.log has real numbers for a step (total input and how much of it came from the cache), the real number counts, which also reveals cache breaks without a pause. In this period that applied to {p} of the steps. Sizes come from text length, images count as a flat amount, and everything is calibrated to the real numbers per session. Sums and total cost are exact, the split into single items is a good approximation.

ses.logged: For {p} of the steps Hermes' log had real numbers.
ses.eats: What ate the most in this session
ses.resume: Continue it in the terminal (tap to select):
ses.steps.hint: History = how many tokens this step had to read. Rebuild = what it cost to write the history into the cache again because it had expired after a pause or was lost without one ({n} times, {cost} in total).
brk.shrunk.why: The prompt got smaller: Hermes removed or rewrote older history, so everything after it was written anew.
brk.image.why: A new image while more than three were in the history: Hermes drops old images from the request, which changes the history.
brk.turn.why: A new message came in and the gateway reloaded the conversation from its database; images stored there as text no longer match.
brk.deep.why: Only the system prompt came from the cache: something more than about 20 blocks back changed, and the cache only looks that far.
brk.other.why: None of the known patterns; the prompt changed somewhere in the middle.
brk.sim.why: No log values for these steps; the replay saw the start of the prompt change (e.g. a plugin or memory block).
proj.hint: Hermes stores no working folder for sessions from Telegram, Discord and cron. So every session counts toward the project whose path shows up most often in its tool calls: folders under /opt and /srv and Git repos in the home folder. “{hermes}” is work on Hermes' own files when no other project shows up. A session across two projects counts fully toward the more frequent one.
set.sub: Stored on this server in data/settings.json. Environment variables only set the defaults.
set.lang.why: Also the language of the push alerts.
set.fx: Costs are API list prices in dollars. Euro uses the ECB reference rate of {date}: 1 € = {rate} $.
set.fx.none: Costs are API list prices in dollars. The ECB rate is not loaded yet, until then amounts stay in dollars.
set.fx.usd: Costs are API list prices in dollars. Euro converts them with the ECB's daily reference rate.
set.period.why: Used when you open a page without picking one.
set.view.why: Numbers and bars on the overview. With “left” the bar and the time mark both run down.
set.cost.why: “% of week” converts API value into a share of your weekly limit. An estimate: Anthropic doesn't publish the exchange rate.
set.src.label: Hermes home
set.src.why: Which Hermes the dashboard reads: the main home or one of its profiles. The limits stay the same, they belong to the account.
set.src.none: No profiles found. Profiles you create with hermes profile create show up here.
set.cost.none: Not enough readings yet: it needs a few hours in which Hermes works and the limit is read.
set.alerts.hint: Each alert comes at most once per limit window, as a push message (set up below).
set.a.five.why: When the window would be full within this many minutes at the pace of the last hour.
set.a.week.why: When the weekly limit runs full before the reset at the current pace. Earliest one day into the week.
set.a.extra.why: When paid extra credits go up.
set.a.extra.steps.why: One alert per month when the used credits pass one of these amounts, e.g. 10, 20. Empty = off.
set.a.free.why: After the window was full, as soon as it resets.
set.a.steps.why: Once per step and week, with the daily budget that is left.
set.a.digest.why: Sunday from 18:00: where the week stands, what Hermes used compared with last week, the biggest eater. Arrives quietly.
set.a.chat.why: When the last three replies of a chat cost at least this share of the week each on average. Every message in a long chat re-reads the whole history, a new chat starts small.
set.a.spike.why: When a cron run or a single reply costs three times its usual amount and at least this share of the week.
set.a.nok: Needs a few days of limit readings first, until then it stays silent.
set.guard.hint: Pauses the cron jobs you mark while the week gets tight and resumes them once there is room again. Jobs you paused yourself stay untouched.
set.guard.on: Pause marked jobs when the week gets tight
set.guard.on.why: Tight means: the week forecast is above 100 % (from the second day on), the week is at 90 % or the 5-hour window at 85 %. Checked every 10 minutes, with a quiet push on every change.
set.guard.jobs.why: Recurring jobs with their cost per week over the last 30 days. One-shot jobs end on their own and are not offered.
set.quiet.why: Alerts wait until the quiet hours are over and only come if they still apply then.
set.push.hint: Alerts arrive through ntfy, a free push app for iPhone and Android. No account needed.
set.push.state.own: Push is on, to your own topic on {server}.
set.push.state.hermes: Push is on, through Hermes' ntfy channel.
set.setup.why: Creates your own random topic on ntfy.sh and turns push on. Takes under a minute.
set.topic.why: Anyone who knows the topic can read along, that is why it is random. Keep it to yourself.
set.ios.1: Install ntfy from the App Store and open it.
set.ios.3: Paste the topic and tap Subscribe.
set.ios.own: For your own server, switch on “Use another server” in that dialog and enter {server}.
set.test.why: Shows right here whether the server took the message.
set.test.auth: The server turned the login down: check the access token under “Own ntfy server”.
set.test.net: The server could not be reached: check the server address and this machine's network.
set.newtopic.why: Creates a new random topic, the old one gets nothing more. Subscribe to the new one afterwards.
set.newtopic.confirm: Create a new topic? Your phone gets nothing more until you subscribe to the new one.
set.own: Own topic (waits while alerts go through Hermes)
set.via.why: “Hermes' ntfy” shares the channel Hermes itself sends to (NTFY_HOME_CHANNEL in ~/.hermes/.env).
set.via.nohermes: “Hermes' ntfy” needs NTFY_HOME_CHANNEL in ~/.hermes/.env, which is not set here.
set.server.why: ntfy.sh is the default. For iPhone push, your own server needs upstream-base-url: "https://ntfy.sh" in its server.yml.
set.token.why: Stored on this server and never shown again. Leave the field empty to keep it.
set.url.why: Opens when you tap an alert.
set.bad: Not saved, these values don't look right: {fields}. The previous values stay.
set.done.setup: Your topic is ready. Subscribe on your phone, then send a test.
set.done.newtopic: New topic created and saved. Subscribe to it on your phone.
